title: New lineups filled with external IP: The vanishing face of Korean games : Business/Industry : JKN

 🌐 한국어 · 日本語 · 中文 · हिन्दी · Español · العربية · Français · বাংলা · Русский · Deutsch Lee Gyeo-rye Reporter 입력 2026.11.14 14:10 ( 연합뉴스 ) Domestic game companies are expanding their lineups by consecutively unveiling new titles based on webtoons and animations. On the other hand, there are limited moves to continue in-house intellectual properties through sequels and remakes, leading to criticism that they must foster long-standing franchises beyond short-term successes.
 Targeting the market with external original works
Netmarble has put forward "Solo Leveling: KARMA" and "Shangri-La Frontier: Seven Best-in-Class" as new titles. Both are scheduled for global release; "KARMA" is being developed as a roguelite action RPG, and "Shangri-La Frontier" as a collectible RPG.
"KARMA" is a spin-off that unfolds the 27-year monarch war not covered in the original work into a game. It is an attempt to attract the fanbase to the game by expanding the gaps in the world rather than just moving the original story as it is. "Shangri-La Frontier" is also based on a Japanese web novel and animation.
Nexon has highlighted "Overgeared," which is based on a Korean game fantasy web novel and webtoon. This title is a massively multiplayer online role-playing game that combines automatic combat with user-versus-user competition, and it held an online showcase in November after beginning pre-registration in October. Webzen and Com2uS have also joined the external IP competition by preparing new titles using web novels, comics, and animations.
 Sustainability beyond the initial launch is key
Utilizing external original works makes it easy to attract user interest based on already well-known worlds and characters. However, there are not many cases among games released based on webtoons and animations that have been serviced for a long time and have grown steadily. This is because if a game fails to secure new content and differentiated gameplay after a surge of users early on, its success can quickly cool down.
Netmarble’s "Solo Leveling: ARISE" is cited as a case that demonstrates this problem. Released in May 2024, it received the Presidential Award at the 2024 Korea Game Awards, but its revenue share was 3% in Netmarble’s third quarter of 2026 data. This means that original work awareness does not immediately lead to long-term game performance.
On the other hand, it is pointed out that domestic game companies are relatively passive in maintaining their own IPs for a long time. It is rare for old titles that are remembered for a long time to be revived through remakes or sequels, even if there are not many users. While there is a reality that it is difficult to maintain less profitable titles in a business structure centered on live-service games, there is concern that assets that can be utilized in the long term may disappear in this process.
 The power of IP shown by long-running series
Large overseas franchises continue their vitality by reinterpreting and expanding existing IPs. Nintendo reconfigured "The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time," released in 1998, with modern graphics, controls, and presentation for the Nintendo Switch 2. This title sold over 5.2 million copies worldwide in the four days following its release.
Bandai Namco’s "Ace Combat" also released its ninth numbered title, "Ace Combat 8: Wings of Deceit," in October to mark the series' 31st anniversary. "GTA" has also maintained its unique identity while changing its gameplay with every series since its first title in 1997.
These cases show that, just as it is important to constantly release new IPs, it is equally important to develop once-created worlds and characters to suit the times. This is why voices are growing that the domestic game industry should come up with strategies to accumulate its own IPs through sequels and remakes while finding new materials in webtoons and animations.
